overview.intro:
Chapter 16 covers meat, fish and seafood that have been cooked, cured, canned or otherwise prepared: sausages, ham, corned beef, prepared chicken, canned tuna and sardines, caviar, cooked shrimp, crab meat and lobster. Its **179 tariff lines** run from Free to 35%. Most cooked shrimp, canned crab meat, lobster and shellfish are Free; prepared chicken and turkey are 6.4%; sardines 15–20%; and tuna in oil carries the chapter's highest rate, **35%**.

The U.S. imported **$7.30B** of these goods in 2025, three-quarters of it seafood: shrimp from India, Vietnam and Indonesia, tuna from Thailand, crab meat from Indonesia. For those suppliers the base rate is rarely the main cost. Since **July 24, 2026** a Section 301 tariff adds 10% or 12.5% for 60 economies, and China pays 37.5% extra on fish and seafood; on a Free line that duty is the whole tariff. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico pay nothing**, and **prepared beef (1602.50)**, most of it from Brazil, is exempt from the Section 301 duties. Food-safety and fisheries rules (USDA, FDA, NOAA) decide whether a shipment can enter at all.

productGroups.label: Sausages
productGroups.blurb: Pork sausages pay 0.8¢/kg, beef sausages in airtight containers 3.4%, and other sausages, including chicken and turkey, 3.2%. Canada and Italy are the main suppliers.

productGroups.label: Prepared meat & poultry (ham, corned beef, chicken)
productGroups.blurb: The meat side of the chapter: ham and pork shoulder (1.4–5.3¢/kg), prepared chicken and turkey (6.4%), corned and cooked beef (Free–4.5%), liver pâté and baby-food meats. Prepared beef is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties.

productGroups.label: Meat & fish extracts and juices
productGroups.blurb: Clam juice pays 8.5%; other meat and fish extracts and juices are Free. A small heading: $29M of imports in 2025.

productGroups.label: Prepared fish & caviar (tuna, sardines, salmon)
productGroups.blurb: Canned tuna is the biggest product: 35% in oil, and 6% within the annual quota or 12.5% above it for other canned tuna. Sardines are 15–20%, caviar 15%, salmon in oil 6%; fish sticks 7.5–10%, and many other fish preparations are Free.

productGroups.label: Prepared crustaceans & molluscs (shrimp, crab, clams)
productGroups.blurb: Cooked shrimp, crab meat in airtight containers, lobster, mussels, squid and octopus are Free. Frozen crab meat not in airtight containers is 5%, oysters 4.7%, and products containing fish meat or prepared meals 5–10%. Shrimp alone was $1.76B of imports in 2025.

workedExamples.title: A $40,000 container of canned tuna in water from Thailand
workedExamples.body: While the 2026 quota (16,364,101 kg) is open, tuna not in oil in cans up to 7 kg is 6%: **$2,400**. Thailand is one of the 60 Section 301 economies, so 12.5% is added (9903.05.77): **$5,000**. Total **$7,400** (18.5%). Once the quota fills the base rate is 12.5% (1604.14.30) and the total is **$10,000** (25%). Packed in oil (1604.14.10) it would be 35% + 12.5% = **$19,000**.

workedExamples.title: $100,000 of cooked frozen shrimp from India
workedExamples.body: Cooked shrimp not in airtight containers is Free under the general rate, so the only tariff is India's 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.44): **$10,000**. If the shrimp is the marinated or dusted kind classified in 1605.21.10.30, it is also within the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on frozen warmwater shrimp from India, and CBP collects a cash deposit at the rate set for the producer. Breaded shrimp (1605.21.10.20) is outside those orders. Every shipment needs the DS-2031 shrimp declaration.

workedExamples.title: $200,000 of canned corned beef from Brazil
workedExamples.body: Corned beef in airtight containers is Free under the general rate, and prepared beef (1602.50) is on the exemption lists of both Brazil Section 301 actions (9903.05.03 and 9903.05.86). The duty is **$0**. A can of Brazilian chicken (1602.32) would pay 6.4% + 25% + 12.5% = **43.9%**. The plant must still be eligible to export to the United States under USDA FSIS rules.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover meat, meat offal, fish, crustaceans, molluscs or other aquatic invertebrates, as well as insects, prepared or preserved by the processes specified in chapter 2 or 3, note 6 to chapter 4 or in heading 0504.

**Note 2.** Food preparations fall in this chapter provided that they contain more than 20 percent by weight of sausage, meat, meat offal, blood, insects, fish or crustaceans, molluscs or other aquatic invertebrates, or any combination thereof. In cases where the preparation contains two or more of the products mentioned above, it is classified in the heading of chapter 16 corresponding to the component or components which predominate by weight. These provisions do not apply to the stuffed products of heading 1902 or the preparations of heading 2103 or 2104.

**Subheading Note 1.** For subheading 1602.10, "homogenized preparations" means preparations of meat, meat offal, blood or insects, finely homogenized, put up for retail sale as food suitable for infants or young children or for dietetic purposes, in containers of a net weight content not exceeding 250 g. This subheading takes precedence over all other subheadings of heading 1602.

**Subheading Note 2.** The fish, crustaceans, molluscs and other aquatic invertebrates named in the subheadings of heading 1604 or 1605 under their common names only are of the same species as those mentioned in chapter 3 under the same name.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**1.** For this chapter, "in oil" means packed in oil or fat, or in added oil or fat and other substances, whether the oil or fat was introduced at the time of packing or before.

**2.** In assessing the duty on meats, no allowance is made for normal components such as bones, fat, and hide or skin. The dutiable weight of meats in airtight containers subject to specific rates includes the entire contents of the containers.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 16: Prepared Meat, Fish and Seafood — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 16 Prepared Meat & Seafood Tariff Updates — What Changed Since January 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 16 (prepared meat, canned tuna, shrimp, crab) since January 2025: base rates on all 179 lines, the end of the IEEPA duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, the beef exemption and the 2026 tuna quota, with Federal Register citations.
keywords: packaged foods and meats tariff changes

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). On every one of the 179 Chapter 16 lines the base rates are the same in both.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate, as extra duties set by country. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada +35%, Mexico +25%, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, prepared meat and seafood from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**, except prepared beef (1602.50), which is on the exemption list. China also pays its older Section 301 duties (**37.5%** extra on fish, seafood and prepared chicken, **20%** on most other meat) and Brazil the separate Brazil Section 301 duty (**37.5%** in all, again except beef). **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are still exempt.**

Outside the tariff, the Marine Mammal Protection Act import bans began on January 1, 2026, and CBP set the 2026 canned-tuna quota on June 3, 2026.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 16 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 lists 3 and 4A, the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 tariff, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. Agency entry rules (FSIS, FDA, NOAA, State) are listed when they changed. Antidumping and countervailing duties on shrimp are noted but not counted. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

The 2025 IEEPA duty on Canada (+35%, 9903.01.10) ended February 24, 2026. No Chapter 16 line is on the 2026 Section 338 duty or import-ban lists for Canada (U.S. note 51).

changes.title: No Chapter 16 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 179 Chapter 16 tariff lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. Revision 21 changed only Chapter 38 and a China exclusion note in Chapter 99.

changes.title: China Section 301 tariffs continue during the second four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so List 3 (25%) and List 4A (7.5%) did not terminate in July 2026 and remain in effect while the statutory review runs. List 3 covers prepared chicken (1602.32), extracts (1603) and all of 1604 and 1605; List 4A covers the other meat preparations and sausages.

changes.title: NOAA starts a review of the MMPA seafood import rules
changes.detail: NOAA Fisheries asked for comments (due September 28, 2026) on revising the Marine Mammal Protection Act import regulations. The current rules, including the import bans that took effect on January 1, 2026, stay in force until any change is adopted.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies reach prepared meat and seafood
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), on 170 of the 179 Chapter 16 lines. The nine lines of prepared beef (1602.50) are on the general exemption list in U.S. note 52(b) (9903.05.86). EU goods pay 10% in total and Japan, South Korea and Switzerland 12.5% in total when the base rate is lower; USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94). Ecuador's tuna loins (1604.14.40) are on its own exception list (note 52(j)).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). Prepared beef (1602.50), including Brazil's canned and cooked beef, is on the exemption list in U.S. note 50(a)(ii) (9903.05.03); every other Chapter 16 line is covered. From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top, again except for 1602.50.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: 2026 canned-tuna quota: 16,364,101 kg at 6%
changes.detail: CBP set the 2026 tariff-rate quota for tuna not in oil in containers up to 7 kg (1604.14.22) at 16,364,101 kg, dutiable at 6% for entries from January 1 through December 31, 2026. Entries above the quota pay 12.5% under 1604.14.30.

changes.title: Swimming crab from Vietnam, Indonesia, Sri Lanka and the Philippines cleared under the MMPA
changes.detail: NOAA Fisheries issued comparability findings for the swimming crab fisheries of Vietnam, Indonesia, Sri Lanka and the Philippines, valid from May 12, 2026 through December 31, 2029, so crab meat from those fisheries (1605.10) may be imported.

changes.title: 2026 Section 609 list of nations certified for wild-caught shrimp
changes.detail: The State Department certified 36 nations and Hong Kong (and particular fisheries of six more) for wild-caught shrimp. From all other nations only farmed shrimp and its products may enter. Every shipment of shrimp or shrimp products needs the DS-2031 declaration.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Prepared beef (1602.50) was on the product exemption list (9903.03.03); USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of prepared meat and seafood rose from **$7.04B in 2024 to $7.30B in 2025** (+3.7%), within the $6.8B–$8.1B range of the last five years. Seafood is three-quarters of the total. Prepared shrimp (1605.21 and 1605.29) alone was **$1.76B**, mostly from India ($554M), Vietnam ($400M) and Indonesia ($372M). Prepared tuna (1604.14) was **$1.19B**, nearly half of it ($567M) from Thailand. Crab meat (1605.10) was $761M, led by Indonesia ($350M).

The meat side runs in two lanes. Canada supplies prepared chicken ($417M of the $512M under 1602.32), and Brazil supplies prepared beef ($449M of the $638M under 1602.50). That is why Canada is the largest single supplier even though most of the chapter is Asian seafood. Among the large suppliers, India (+22%), Ecuador (+25%) and Poland (+33%) grew fastest; China fell 21%, to $223M.

These are 2025 figures, when the IEEPA duties applied. Those ended on February 24, 2026, and the 2026 Section 301 duties started only on July 24, 2026, so their effect is not in the data yet. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on prepared meat and seafood depends as much on **where it comes from** as on what it is. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference, taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free**. Thailand and Vietnam add 12.5%, Indonesia, India and Ecuador 10%, and EU goods, such as Poland's fish preparations, pay **10% in total** unless the base rate is higher. **China adds 37.5% on seafood** and 20% on most meat. **Prepared beef is exempt** from the 2026 action, so Brazil's corned beef keeps its base rate while other Brazilian goods pay +37.5%.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 16: Prepared Meat, Fish and Seafood — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Prepared Meat & Seafood: FSIS, FDA, NOAA Rules & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 16) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The documents and agency rules for each HTS Chapter 16 line — USDA FSIS meat inspection, FDA seafood HACCP and canned-food filing, NOAA tuna and seafood monitoring, shrimp DS-2031 — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, FTAs, the canned-tuna quota, rulings and drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For prepared meat and seafood the paperwork decides whether a shipment clears at all. **Meat and poultry** need a plant USDA FSIS has found eligible and reinspection on arrival; **fish and seafood** fall under FDA's seafood HACCP rules, and canned products need a filed process. Tuna, shrimp and crab add NOAA and State Department documents.

The ways to pay less are in the schedule: claim **USMCA** or another **FTA**, watch the **canned-tuna quota**, get a **ruling** on borderline classifications, and use **drawback** when goods are re-exported. Each one depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian or Mexican goods plus the base rate (up to 6.4% or a few cents per kg on Chapter 16 lines)
levers.appliesTo: All 179 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: The goods must meet the USMCA rule of origin for their subheading; a preparation made from non-originating meat or fish may not qualify. A claim without a valid certification exposes the entry to the 10% Section 301 duty plus penalties. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim another free trade agreement on the base rate
levers.saves: The base rate: 35% on tuna in oil, 12.5% or 6% on other canned tuna, 15–20% on sardines, 6.4% on poultry and many meat preparations. The Section 301 duty for the country stays.
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines, for originating goods of an FTA partner listed in the Special column (Chile, Peru, Colombia, Korea, Australia, the CAFTA-DR countries and others)
levers.document: The proof of origin each agreement requires (for most, an importer claim backed by a certification and records), with the SPI code on the entry.
levers.caveat: U.S. note 52(a) to Chapter 99 keeps the 2026 Section 301 duty when an FTA rate is claimed, so a Chilean or Peruvian preparation still pays +12.5%. GSP (A, A+, A*) has been expired since December 31, 2020 and gives no relief.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Know the canned-tuna quota tier before you price a shipment
levers.saves: Up to 6.5 points: tuna not in oil in containers up to 7 kg pays 6% within the 2026 quota (1604.14.22) and 12.5% once it fills (1604.14.30). Tuna in oil pays 35% (1604.14.10).
levers.appliesTo: Canned and pouched tuna and skipjack, 1604.14.10–1604.14.30
levers.document: Nothing to file: CBP applies the in-quota rate to entries until the 2026 quota of 16,364,101 kg is reached, then the over-quota rate. Check the CBP quota bulletins for the fill status.
levers.caveat: The quota is first-come, first-served across all importers for the calendar year. Any Section 301 duty for the country is added on top in both tiers. Whether tuna is "in oil" depends on the packing medium (Chapter 16 additional U.S. note 1), not the label.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 16, Additional U.S. Notes 1 and 3

levers.title: Get a binding ruling on borderline classifications
levers.saves: Certainty on where a product falls: a food preparation is in Chapter 16 only if it contains more than 20% by weight of meat, fish or seafood (Chapter 16 note 2), and "in oil", "in airtight containers" and "prepared meals" change the rate within a heading
levers.appliesTo: Mixed preparations, meal kits, breaded or battered seafood, tuna and other fish in different packing media
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its ingredients by weight and its packing.
levers.caveat: A ruling applies to the product described. It also matters outside the tariff: the shrimp antidumping and countervailing duty orders cover some 1605 shrimp lines but exclude breaded, canned and prepared-meal shrimp, and Commerce decides scope by the written description, not the HTS number.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods that are exported or destroyed
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid on imported goods that are later exported or destroyed, or used to make exported goods
levers.appliesTo: Any line, when the imported preparation (or an article made from it) leaves the United States
levers.document: A drawback claim filed with CBP in ACE, with import and export records that link the goods.
levers.caveat: Drawback has strict filing deadlines and recordkeeping. Check the Chapter 99 note of each extra duty for whether it can be drawn back before relying on it.

rules.title: Meat products: only from countries and plants FSIS has found equivalent, with a foreign inspection certificate, and reinspected at an official import inspection establishment
Poultry products (chicken, turkey, duck, goose): only from countries FSIS has found eligible for poultry, with a foreign inspection certificate and reinspection
Catfish (Siluriformes) products: FSIS equivalence and reinspection, as for meat

Animal-disease limits on meat from regions with foot-and-mouth disease, African or classical swine fever, swine vesicular disease, HPAI or Newcastle disease: only cooked, cured or canned products that meet the processing conditions, with certificates
Fish and seafood: importer must verify the foreign processor follows seafood HACCP (21 CFR part 123); these products are exempt from FSVP when the supplier complies with part 123
All FDA-regulated food: registered foreign facility and prior notice before arrival
Canned fish and shellfish (low-acid canned foods): registered processing plant and filed scheduled process for each product
China and Hong Kong: aquacultured shrimp, dace and eel (including breaded, smoked and processed) detained without examination unless the firm is on the green list (Import Alert 16-131)

Seafood Import Monitoring Program: International Fisheries Trade Permit and harvest and chain-of-custody data at entry for tuna, shrimp, blue and king crab, cod, abalone, sea cucumber and other covered species
Tuna: Fisheries Certificate of Origin (NOAA Form 370) and dolphin-safe statements filed electronically with CBP at entry
Marine Mammal Protection Act: since January 1, 2026 fish and fish products from fisheries without a comparability finding cannot be imported; similar products need a Certification of Admissibility

citations.label: 90 FR 42395: comparability findings and import restrictions (September 2, 2025)

rules.title: Shrimp and products containing shrimp: DS-2031 Shrimp Exporter's/Importer's Declaration; wild-caught shrimp only from nations or fisheries certified under Section 609 (HTS Ch. 16 statistical note 1)

Antidumping and countervailing duties on frozen warmwater shrimp, including dusted and marinated shrimp under 1605.21.10.30 and 1605.29.10.10 (breaded, canned and prepared-meal shrimp excluded): cash deposits by producer on top of the tariff

citations.label: 89 FR 104982: Indonesia AD order; Ecuador, India, Vietnam CVD orders (December 26, 2024)

rules.title: Sturgeon caviar: CITES export permit and Form 3-177 declaration at entry
Russia: fish, seafood and preparations of Russian origin may not be imported, including Russian-caught fish processed in another country

groups.label: Sausages
groups.note: Sausages of beef, pork or other meat follow the FSIS meat rules; chicken or turkey sausages follow the poultry rules. Pork sausages from regions with African or classical swine fever must meet the APHIS cooking conditions.

groups.label: Prepared meat & poultry (ham, corned beef, chicken)
groups.note: Every meat line needs an FSIS-eligible country and plant. Poultry lines (1602.31–1602.39) follow the poultry rules; frog meat (1602.90.10) falls to FDA instead.

groups.label: Meat & fish extracts and juices
groups.note: Clam juice and fish extracts are FDA-regulated seafood; meat extracts generally fall under FSIS.

groups.label: Prepared fish & caviar (tuna, sardines, salmon)
groups.note: Canned fish adds the FDA low-acid canned food rules; tuna adds NOAA Form 370 and the Seafood Import Monitoring Program; catfish preparations go to FSIS; sturgeon caviar needs CITES documents.

groups.label: Prepared crustaceans & molluscs (shrimp, crab, clams)
groups.note: Shrimp adds the DS-2031 declaration, the Seafood Import Monitoring Program and, for some lines and countries, antidumping or countervailing duties. Crab meat, abalone and sea cucumber are also covered by the Seafood Import Monitoring Program.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations — not legal advice. Eligibility lists, MMPA findings and Section 609 certifications change; check FSIS, FDA and NOAA before each shipment.

finalConclusion.h1: HTS Chapter 16: Prepared Meat, Fish and Seafood — Tariff FAQ

seo.title: Prepared Meat & Seafood Tariffs FAQ: Canned Tuna, Shrimp from India, China, Canada, HS Codes (HTS Ch. 16) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about prepared meat and seafood tariffs: the canned tuna tariff and HS code, tariffs on seafood from China, Canada and India, corned beef, sausage, crab meat and cooked shrimp HS codes, caviar.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing prepared meat, fish and seafood into the U.S.: tariffs by country, HS codes and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free: no base rate and no extra duty.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty is a Section 301 tariff: +10% or +12.5% for 60 economies (10% in total for the EU), +37.5% on Chinese seafood. Prepared beef (1602.50) is exempt.
Much of the chapter is Free at base, so for cooked shrimp, crab meat and lobster the Section 301 duty is the whole tariff. Canned tuna is the exception: 35% in oil, 6% or 12.5% otherwise.

Entry rules decide whether a shipment lands: FSIS eligibility for meat, FDA seafood HACCP and canned-food filings, NOAA documents for tuna and shrimp, and the MMPA import bans in force since January 1, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on canned tuna, and what is its HS code?
searchedAs: hs code for canned tuna in oil
faqs.answer: Canned tuna is HS 1604.14. Tuna in oil (1604.14.10) is 35%. Other tuna in airtight containers up to 7 kg (1604.14.22) pays 6% on the first 16,364,101 kg entered in 2026 and 12.5% once that quota fills (1604.14.30). Since July 24, 2026 most large suppliers also pay a Section 301 duty: +12.5% for Thailand (the largest, $567M of prepared tuna in 2025), Vietnam and the Philippines, +10% for Ecuador and Indonesia, and +37.5% for China. USMCA-qualifying tuna from Mexico pays nothing.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on seafood imports in 2026?
faqs.answer: Yes. For prepared seafood (headings 1604 and 1605) the base rate applies, and since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff adds 10% or 12.5% for 60 economies, including Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, India and Ecuador. China pays 37.5% extra. Many items are Free at base, such as cooked shrimp, crab meat in airtight containers and lobster, so the Section 301 duty is the whole tariff. The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Fresh and frozen raw seafood is in Chapter 3, not here.

faqs.question: Are there U.S. tariffs on Canadian seafood?
faqs.answer: Not on goods that qualify for USMCA: they are exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian products (9903.05.93), and prepared lobster and crab are Free at base. Canadian goods that do not qualify pay the base rate plus 10% (9903.05.29). The 35% IEEPA duty of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026. Canada shipped $466M of prepared crustaceans and molluscs (1605) to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on seafood from China?
faqs.answer: Prepared fish and seafood from China pay the base rate plus 37.5%: 25% under Section 301 List 3 (9903.88.03) and 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.31). Cooked shrimp or canned crab meat (Free base) pays 37.5%; tuna in oil pays 72.5%. Four kinds of crab meat in airtight containers can be excluded from the 25% through November 9, 2026. FDA also detains aquacultured shrimp and eel from China unless the firm is on its green list (Import Alert 16-131). U.S. imports of Chapter 16 goods from China fell 21% to $223M in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on shrimp from India?
faqs.answer: Cooked and prepared shrimp (1605.21, 1605.29) is Free at base, so India pays its 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.44). Marinated or dusted frozen shrimp (1605.21.10.30, 1605.29.10.10) is also within the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on frozen warmwater shrimp from India, so CBP collects a cash deposit at the producer's rate; breaded and canned shrimp are outside those orders. India was the largest supplier of prepared shrimp in 2025 ($554M). Raw frozen shrimp is classified in Chapter 3 (0306.17).

faqs.question: What is the tariff code for corned beef, and what duty does it pay?
faqs.answer: Corned beef in airtight containers is 1602.50.07 and is Free; other cured or pickled beef is 1602.50.08 at 4.5%. Prepared beef is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties (9903.05.86) and the Brazil Section 301 duty (9903.05.03), so canned corned beef from Brazil, the largest supplier ($449M of prepared beef in 2025), still enters free. China's List 4A adds 7.5%. The plant must be eligible under USDA FSIS rules (9 CFR 327.2).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for sausage?
faqs.answer: Heading 1601. Pork sausages are 1601.00.20 (0.8¢/kg); beef sausages in airtight containers are 1601.00.40 (3.4%); all other sausages, including chicken and turkey, are 1601.00.60 (3.2%). Sausage casings are not in this chapter. Imports must come from plants USDA FSIS has found eligible, and pork sausages from regions with African swine fever must meet APHIS cooking rules (9 CFR 94.8).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for crab meat?
faqs.answer: 1605.10. Crab meat in airtight containers, such as pasteurized crab meat, is 1605.10.20 (Free); other crab meat, such as frozen crab meat not in airtight containers, is 1605.10.40 (5%); crab products containing fish meat and prepared meals are 1605.10.05 (10%). A Section 301 duty for the country is added, for example +10% for Indonesia, the largest supplier ($350M in 2025). Blue and king crab are also covered by NOAA's Seafood Import Monitoring Program.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for cooked shrimp?
searchedAs: hs code for frozen cooked shrimp
faqs.answer: Cooked or otherwise prepared shrimp is 1605.21 when not in airtight containers and 1605.29 when canned or in other airtight containers; both are Free unless the product contains fish meat or is a prepared meal (5%). Breaded frozen shrimp is 1605.21.10.20. Raw frozen shrimp, including shell-on and peeled, is 0306.17 in Chapter 3. Every shrimp shipment needs the DS-2031 declaration.

faqs.question: What do HS codes 1604 and 1605 cover?
faqs.answer: 1604 is prepared or preserved fish and caviar: salmon (1604.11), herring (1604.12), sardines (1604.13), tuna (1604.14), mackerel (1604.15), anchovies (1604.16), other fish (1604.19), fish sticks, surimi and other fish preparations (1604.20) and caviar (1604.31). 1605 is prepared crustaceans and molluscs: crab (1605.10), shrimp (1605.21, 1605.29), lobster (1605.30), and oysters, scallops, mussels, squid, octopus, clams, abalone and sea cucumbers (1605.51–1605.69).

faqs.question: What does HS code 1602 cover?
faqs.answer: Prepared or preserved meat other than sausages: homogenized baby-food meats (1602.10), liver (1602.20), turkey (1602.31), chicken (1602.32), other poultry (1602.39), ham (1602.41), pork shoulder (1602.42), other pork (1602.49), beef (1602.50) and other meat (1602.90). Prepared chicken (6.4%) came mostly from Canada ($417M in 2025) and prepared beef (Free–4.5%) mostly from Brazil.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on caviar?
faqs.answer: Caviar (1604.31) is 15%; caviar substitutes (1604.32) are Free. For EU caviar the 15% base rate is above the 10% EU Section 301 floor, so it pays 15% alone; China pays 15% + 37.5%. Sturgeon caviar also needs CITES documents from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The U.S. imported $66.5M of caviar in 2025.
